MEDICAL SUPPORT: HEALTH INSURANCE COVERAGE ORDERS AND ASSIGNMENTS IN A CALIFORNIA CHILD SUPPORT CASE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Marisol Iyabo Ferreira · Dmitri Anselm Ferreira

PARTIES, SCOPE, AND PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This Medical Support Information Sheet concerns Marisol Iyabo Ferreira and Dmitri Anselm Ferreira, the child or children identified as Ilse Ferreira and Caspian Ferreira, and the pending child support proceeding and the health insurance provisions of any support order made in it, a matter pending or to be filed in the California superior court for Stanislaus. California child support law is usually described as a law about money: how much one parent pays the other each month, how that figure is computed, and what happens when it is not paid. Chapter 7 of Part 1 of Division 9 of the Family Code, sections 3750 through 3773, is about something else. It requires that a support order also settle who insures the child's health, it fixes a numeric test for when that insurance counts as affordable, and it supplies a separate enforcement instrument -- a health insurance coverage assignment served on an employer -- that operates independently of any order to pay money. This sheet surveys the two articles of that chapter: Article 1 (sections 3750 to 3753), which governs the order itself, and Article 2 (sections 3760 to 3773), which governs the assignment to the employer, the obligor's motion to quash, the employer's duties and liabilities, and the national medical support notice used in Title IV-D cases. It also surveys the two mandatory Judicial Council forms adopted under section 3772, forms FL-470 and FL-478, and the federal provisions the chapter incorporates, 42 U.S.C. section 666(a)(19) and section 609(a)(5)(C) of the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974, 29 U.S.C. section 1169(a)(5)(C). It states what those authorities say. It does not determine whether any order, assignment or notice is required, available or valid in this case, does not recommend that any of them be sought, opposed, quashed or terminated, does not compute any amount, does not predict how a court or a plan administrator would rule, and is not a substitute for advice from a lawyer licensed in California.

THE REQUIREMENT THAT A SUPPORT ORDER ADDRESS HEALTH INSURANCE, AND WHAT "HEALTH INSURANCE COVERAGE" MEANS
Family Code section 3751 places two distinct requirements on a child support order. The first, in subdivision (a)(1), is informational and runs to the government: support orders issued or modified under Chapter 7 must include a provision requiring the child support obligor to keep the Title IV-D agency informed of whether the obligor has health insurance coverage at a reasonable cost and, if so, the policy information. The second, in subdivision (a)(2), is substantive: when an amount is set for current support, the court is directed to require that health insurance coverage for a supported child be maintained by either or both parents if that insurance is available at no cost or at a reasonable cost to the parent. The obligation is not limited to the paying parent; the statute names "either or both parents." What counts as covered is defined broadly and in two places. Section 3750, which governs Article 1, provides that health insurance coverage includes vision care and dental care coverage, whether part of an existing policy or issued separately, and includes the delivery of health care services through a fee-for-service arrangement, a health maintenance organization, a preferred provider organization, or any other type of health care delivery system under which medical services could be provided to a dependent child of an absent parent. Section 3760 repeats that vision and dental inclusion for Article 2 and adds that "employer" reaches the United States government and any public entity as defined in Government Code section 811.2.

THE FIVE PERCENT TEST FOR "REASONABLE COST," AND THE LOW-INCOME ADJUSTMENT OVERRIDE
Section 3751(a)(2) supplies a numeric presumption rather than a standard left to discretion. Health insurance coverage is rebuttably presumed to be reasonable in cost if the cost to the responsible parent providing medical support does not exceed 5 percent of the parent's gross income. The statute then fixes what "the cost" means for that calculation: in applying the 5 percent, the cost is the difference between self-only and family coverage -- the incremental cost of adding dependents, not the whole premium. The same subdivision carries an override running the other way. If the obligor is entitled to the low-income adjustment provided in Family Code section 4055(b)(7), medical support is deemed not reasonable, unless the court determines that not requiring medical support would be unjust and inappropriate in the particular case. Two findings are tied to statements on the record: if the court determines that the cost of health insurance coverage is not reasonable, it is directed to state its reasons on the record, and if it determines that, although the obligor is entitled to a low-income adjustment, not requiring medical support would be unjust and inappropriate, it is likewise directed to state its reasons on the record.

THE STANDING ORDER FOR COVERAGE THAT DOES NOT YET EXIST, AND COVERAGE PAST THE LIMITING AGE
Section 3751 does not treat unavailability of insurance as the end of the subject. Subdivision (b) provides that if the court determines coverage is not available at no cost or at a reasonable cost, the support order must contain a provision specifying that coverage shall be obtained if it becomes available at no cost or at a reasonable cost, and that upon such coverage becoming available to a parent, the parent shall apply for it. The obligation is therefore continuing and self-executing in form: it is written into the original order and is triggered by a later change in the parent's circumstances rather than by a new court hearing. Subdivision (c) addresses the other end of the timeline. The support order must require the parent who provides health insurance coverage for a supported child, whether at the time of the order or afterwards, to seek continuation of coverage for the child upon the child's attainment of the limiting age for a dependent child under that coverage, if the child meets the criteria specified under Health and Safety Code section 1373 or Insurance Code section 10277 or 10278 and the coverage is available at no cost or at a reasonable cost to the parent or parents, as applicable. The cross-referenced provisions concern continued coverage for a dependent child who is incapable of self-sustaining employment by reason of a physically or mentally disabling condition; this sheet does not reproduce or summarize those provisions, which are in other codes and were not fetched for it.

WHERE THE PREMIUM SITS IN RELATION TO THE GUIDELINE AMOUNT
Section 3753 places the cost of the health insurance outside the guideline figure rather than inside it. The cost of the health insurance is to be in addition to the child support amount ordered under Article 2 of Chapter 2 of Part 2 of Division 9, the guideline article beginning at Family Code section 4050, with allowance for the costs of health insurance actually obtained given due consideration under Family Code section 4059(d). Two features of that sentence are worth separating. The direction that the cost be "in addition to" the guideline amount is unqualified. The reference to section 4059(d), by contrast, points to the deductions used in computing annual net disposable income, and the statute frames it as "due consideration" of costs "actually obtained" rather than as an automatic adjustment. The present text of section 3753 was not amended into the code but repealed and re-added by Statutes 1994, chapter 1269, section 36, effective January 1, 1995.

RULES AIMED AT INSURERS AND EMPLOYERS RATHER THAN AT PARENTS: SECTION 3751.5
Section 3751.5 sits in Article 1 but regulates private parties who are not before the family court. Subdivision (a) forbids an employer or insurer to deny enrollment of a child under a parent's health insurance coverage on any of three grounds: that the child was born out of wedlock, that the child is not claimed as a dependent on the parent's federal income tax return, or that the child does not reside with the parent or within the insurer's service area. Subdivision (b) applies where a parent is required by a court or administrative order to provide coverage and is eligible for family coverage through an employer or insurer. In that situation the employer or insurer must permit the parent to enroll any child otherwise eligible without regard to any enrollment period restrictions, and, if the parent is enrolled but fails to apply to obtain coverage of the child, must enroll the child upon presentation of the court order or on request by the local child support agency, the other parent or person having custody of the child, or the Medi-Cal program. The same subdivision limits disenrollment: coverage of a child may not be dropped unless the employer has eliminated family coverage for all its employees, or the employer or insurer receives satisfactory written evidence either that the order is no longer in effect or has been terminated under section 3770, or that the child is or will be enrolled in comparable coverage through another insurer taking effect no later than the effective date of the disenrollment. Subdivision (c) requires the insurer to give the noncovered parent or other person having custody, and the local child support agency on request, the child's membership or identification card, the evidence of coverage and disclosure form, and other coverage information provided to the covered parent.

THE SECOND INSTRUMENT: APPLYING FOR A HEALTH INSURANCE COVERAGE ASSIGNMENT
Article 2 supplies an enforcement device that does not depend on the obligor's cooperation. Section 3761(a) provides that upon application by a party or the local child support agency in any proceeding where the court has ordered either or both parents to maintain coverage under Article 1, the court shall order the obligor's employer, or other person providing health insurance to the obligor, to enroll the supported child in the plan available to the obligor and to deduct the appropriate premium or costs, if any, from the obligor's earnings, unless the court makes a finding of good cause for not making the order. Section 3760(c) gives that order its name: a "health insurance coverage assignment" or "assignment order" is an order made under section 3761. The application is conditioned on advance warning. Section 3761(b)(1) requires the application to state that the applicant gave the obligor written notice of intent to seek an assignment order in the event of a default in instituting court-ordered coverage, and that the notice was transmitted by first-class mail, postage prepaid, or personally served at least 15 days before the application was filed. The notice may be given when a petition or complaint for support is filed or at any later time, and the obligor may waive it at any time. Section 3761(b)(2) requires the applicant to file a certificate of service showing the method and date of service of the order and of the statements required by section 3772 on the employer or insurance provider. Section 3761(c) caps the deduction: the total that may be withheld from earnings for all obligations, including health insurance assignments, is limited by Code of Civil Procedure section 706.052(a) or 15 U.S.C. section 1673, whichever is less.

WHAT "GOOD CAUSE" IS LIMITED TO, WHOM THE ASSIGNMENT BINDS, AND WHEN IT TAKES EFFECT
Three short sections define the assignment's boundaries. WHAT THE EMPLOYER MUST DO, AND WHICH PLAN THE CHILD GOES INTO
Section 3766 tells the employer or other person providing health insurance when to act and how to choose a plan. THE OBLIGOR'S MOTION TO QUASH: SIX ENUMERATED GROUNDS AND A FIFTEEN-DAY CLOCK
Section 3765 is the obligor's route of objection, and it is closed-ended on its face. The obligor may move to quash a health insurance coverage assignment order if the obligor declares under penalty of perjury that there is error on any of the following grounds: that no order to maintain health insurance has been issued under Article 1; that the amount to be withheld for premiums is greater than that permissible under Article 1 or greater than the amount otherwise ordered by the court; that the amount of the increased premium is unreasonable; that the alleged obligor is not the obligor from whom coverage is due; that the child is or will be otherwise provided health care coverage; or that the employer's choice of coverage is inappropriate. The motion and notice of motion, including the declaration, must be filed with the court that issued the assignment order within 15 days after delivery of a copy of the order to the obligor under section 3764(b). The clerk sets the motion for hearing not less than 15 nor more than 30 days after receiving the notice of motion, and within five days of receipt delivers a copy of the notice of motion to the district attorney personally or by first-class mail and, by first-class mail, to the applicant and to the employer or other person providing health insurance at the addresses in the application. Subdivision (c) states the consequence: upon a finding of error described in subdivision (a), the court shall quash the assignment.

Form FL-478, Request and Notice of Hearing Regarding Health Insurance Assignment, is a form adopted for mandatory use by the Judicial Council and cites Family Code sections 3761, 3765 and 3773 as its authority. The form also offers an unlimited "Other (specify)" box. ENDING THE ASSIGNMENT, AND WHAT HAPPENS TO AN EMPLOYER WHO IGNORES IT
Three sections close out Article 2. Section 3770 provides that on notice of motion by the obligor the court shall terminate a health insurance coverage assignment order if any of four conditions exists: a new order has issued under Article 1 that is inconsistent with the existing assignment; the employer or other person providing health insurance has discontinued that coverage to the obligor; the court determines there is good cause, consistent with section 3762, to terminate; or the child for whom the insurance was obtained has died or become emancipated. Section 3768 supplies the consequences of disregarding an assignment. An employer or other person providing health insurance who willfully fails to comply with a valid assignment order entered and served under Article 2 is liable to the applicant for the amount incurred in health care services that would otherwise have been covered under the policy but for the conduct contrary to the order, and willful failure to comply is punishable as contempt of court under Code of Civil Procedure section 1218. Section 3769 protects the employee: no employer may use an assignment order as grounds for refusing to hire a person or for discharging or taking disciplinary action against an employee, and an employer who violates the section may be assessed a civil penalty of a maximum of five hundred dollars. Section 3771 adds an information channel: on request of the local child support agency the employer must provide, within 30 days, the absent parent's social security number and home address, whether the parent has a health insurance policy and if so the policy names and numbers and the persons covered, and whether the policy covers dependent children who do not live in the parent's home; subdivision (e) then requires the employer to notify the agency of any subsequent lapse in coverage, with the date coverage ended, the reason, and the expected resumption date if the lapse is temporary.

Section 3773 creates a parallel track that applies only to Title IV-D cases in which support enforcement services are being provided by the local child support agency under Family Code section 17400. expectedJSON.body: This Medical Support Information Sheet concerns Marisol Iyabo Ferreira and Dmitri Anselm Ferreira, the child or children identified as Ilse Ferreira and Caspian Ferreira, and the pending child support proceeding and the health insurance provisions of any support order made in it, a matter pending or to be filed in the California superior court for Stanislaus. California child support law is usually described as a law about money: how much one parent pays the other each month, how that figure is computed, and what happens when it is not paid. Chapter 7 of Part 1 of Division 9 of the Family Code, sections 3750 through 3773, is about something else. It requires that a support order also settle who insures the child's health, it fixes a numeric test for when that insurance counts as affordable, and it supplies a separate enforcement instrument -- a health insurance coverage assignment served on an employer -- that operates independently of any order to pay money. This sheet surveys the two articles of that chapter: Article 1 (sections 3750 to 3753), which governs the order itself, and Article 2 (sections 3760 to 3773), which governs the assignment to the employer, the obligor's motion to quash, the employer's duties and liabilities, and the national medical support notice used in Title IV-D cases. It also surveys the two mandatory Judicial Council forms adopted under section 3772, forms FL-470 and FL-478, and the federal provisions the chapter incorporates, 42 U.S.C. section 666(a)(19) and section 609(a)(5)(C) of the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974, 29 U.S.C. section 1169(a)(5)(C). It states what those authorities say. It does not determine whether any order, assignment or notice is required, available or valid in this case, does not recommend that any of them be sought, opposed, quashed or terminated, does not compute any amount, does not predict how a court or a plan administrator would rule, and is not a substitute for advice from a lawyer licensed in California.

Family Code section 3751 places two distinct requirements on a child support order. The first, in subdivision (a)(1), is informational and runs to the government: support orders issued or modified under Chapter 7 must include a provision requiring the child support obligor to keep the Title IV-D agency informed of whether the obligor has health insurance coverage at a reasonable cost and, if so, the policy information. The second, in subdivision (a)(2), is substantive: when an amount is set for current support, the court is directed to require that health insurance coverage for a supported child be maintained by either or both parents if that insurance is available at no cost or at a reasonable cost to the parent. The obligation is not limited to the paying parent; the statute names "either or both parents." What counts as covered is defined broadly and in two places. Section 3750, which governs Article 1, provides that health insurance coverage includes vision care and dental care coverage, whether part of an existing policy or issued separately, and includes the delivery of health care services through a fee-for-service arrangement, a health maintenance organization, a preferred provider organization, or any other type of health care delivery system under which medical services could be provided to a dependent child of an absent parent. Section 3760 repeats that vision and dental inclusion for Article 2 and adds that "employer" reaches the United States government and any public entity as defined in Government Code section 811.2.

expectedJSON.body: Section 3751(a)(2) supplies a numeric presumption rather than a standard left to discretion. Health insurance coverage is rebuttably presumed to be reasonable in cost if the cost to the responsible parent providing medical support does not exceed 5 percent of the parent's gross income. The statute then fixes what "the cost" means for that calculation: in applying the 5 percent, the cost is the difference between self-only and family coverage -- the incremental cost of adding dependents, not the whole premium. The same subdivision carries an override running the other way. If the obligor is entitled to the low-income adjustment provided in Family Code section 4055(b)(7), medical support is deemed not reasonable, unless the court determines that not requiring medical support would be unjust and inappropriate in the particular case. Two findings are tied to statements on the record: if the court determines that the cost of health insurance coverage is not reasonable, it is directed to state its reasons on the record, and if it determines that, although the obligor is entitled to a low-income adjustment, not requiring medical support would be unjust and inappropriate, it is likewise directed to state its reasons on the record.

expectedJSON.body: Section 3751 does not treat unavailability of insurance as the end of the subject. Subdivision (b) provides that if the court determines coverage is not available at no cost or at a reasonable cost, the support order must contain a provision specifying that coverage shall be obtained if it becomes available at no cost or at a reasonable cost, and that upon such coverage becoming available to a parent, the parent shall apply for it. The obligation is therefore continuing and self-executing in form: it is written into the original order and is triggered by a later change in the parent's circumstances rather than by a new court hearing. Subdivision (c) addresses the other end of the timeline. The support order must require the parent who provides health insurance coverage for a supported child, whether at the time of the order or afterwards, to seek continuation of coverage for the child upon the child's attainment of the limiting age for a dependent child under that coverage, if the child meets the criteria specified under Health and Safety Code section 1373 or Insurance Code section 10277 or 10278 and the coverage is available at no cost or at a reasonable cost to the parent or parents, as applicable. The cross-referenced provisions concern continued coverage for a dependent child who is incapable of self-sustaining employment by reason of a physically or mentally disabling condition; this sheet does not reproduce or summarize those provisions, which are in other codes and were not fetched for it.

expectedJSON.body: Section 3751.5 sits in Article 1 but regulates private parties who are not before the family court. Subdivision (a) forbids an employer or insurer to deny enrollment of a child under a parent's health insurance coverage on any of three grounds: that the child was born out of wedlock, that the child is not claimed as a dependent on the parent's federal income tax return, or that the child does not reside with the parent or within the insurer's service area. Subdivision (b) applies where a parent is required by a court or administrative order to provide coverage and is eligible for family coverage through an employer or insurer. In that situation the employer or insurer must permit the parent to enroll any child otherwise eligible without regard to any enrollment period restrictions, and, if the parent is enrolled but fails to apply to obtain coverage of the child, must enroll the child upon presentation of the court order or on request by the local child support agency, the other parent or person having custody of the child, or the Medi-Cal program. The same subdivision limits disenrollment: coverage of a child may not be dropped unless the employer has eliminated family coverage for all its employees, or the employer or insurer receives satisfactory written evidence either that the order is no longer in effect or has been terminated under section 3770, or that the child is or will be enrolled in comparable coverage through another insurer taking effect no later than the effective date of the disenrollment. Subdivision (c) requires the insurer to give the noncovered parent or other person having custody, and the local child support agency on request, the child's membership or identification card, the evidence of coverage and disclosure form, and other coverage information provided to the covered parent.

expectedJSON.body: Article 2 supplies an enforcement device that does not depend on the obligor's cooperation. Section 3761(a) provides that upon application by a party or the local child support agency in any proceeding where the court has ordered either or both parents to maintain coverage under Article 1, the court shall order the obligor's employer, or other person providing health insurance to the obligor, to enroll the supported child in the plan available to the obligor and to deduct the appropriate premium or costs, if any, from the obligor's earnings, unless the court makes a finding of good cause for not making the order. Section 3760(c) gives that order its name: a "health insurance coverage assignment" or "assignment order" is an order made under section 3761. The application is conditioned on advance warning. Section 3761(b)(1) requires the application to state that the applicant gave the obligor written notice of intent to seek an assignment order in the event of a default in instituting court-ordered coverage, and that the notice was transmitted by first-class mail, postage prepaid, or personally served at least 15 days before the application was filed. The notice may be given when a petition or complaint for support is filed or at any later time, and the obligor may waive it at any time. Section 3761(b)(2) requires the applicant to file a certificate of service showing the method and date of service of the order and of the statements required by section 3772 on the employer or insurance provider. Section 3761(c) caps the deduction: the total that may be withheld from earnings for all obligations, including health insurance assignments, is limited by Code of Civil Procedure section 706.052(a) or 15 U.S.C. section 1673, whichever is less.

expectedJSON.body: Three short sections define the assignment's boundaries. Section 3762 closes the good-cause exception that section 3761(a) opens: good cause for not making an assignment order is limited to either of two things -- a finding that one of the conditions listed in section 3765(a) or in section 3770 exists, or a finding that the order would cause extraordinary hardship to the obligor, in which case the court is directed to specify the nature of the hardship and, whenever possible, a date by which the obligor shall obtain coverage or be subject to an assignment. Section 3763(a) fixes the timing and reach of the order: it may be ordered at the time of trial or entry of a judgment ordering health insurance coverage, it operates as an assignment, and it binds any existing or future employer of the obligor parent, or other person providing health insurance to the obligor, on whom a copy has been served. Section 3763(b) adds that the order of assignment may be modified at any time by the court. Section 3764 sets the service sequence. The assignment order does not become effective until 20 days after the applicant serves it on the employer. Within 10 days after service of the order, the employer or other person providing health insurance must deliver a copy to the obligor together with a written statement of the obligor's rights and the relevant procedures for moving to quash. Service on the employer or other provider may be made by first-class mail in the manner prescribed by Code of Civil Procedure section 1013.

expectedJSON.body: Three sections close out Article 2. Section 3770 provides that on notice of motion by the obligor the court shall terminate a health insurance coverage assignment order if any of four conditions exists: a new order has issued under Article 1 that is inconsistent with the existing assignment; the employer or other person providing health insurance has discontinued that coverage to the obligor; the court determines there is good cause, consistent with section 3762, to terminate; or the child for whom the insurance was obtained has died or become emancipated. Section 3768 supplies the consequences of disregarding an assignment. An employer or other person providing health insurance who willfully fails to comply with a valid assignment order entered and served under Article 2 is liable to the applicant for the amount incurred in health care services that would otherwise have been covered under the policy but for the conduct contrary to the order, and willful failure to comply is punishable as contempt of court under Code of Civil Procedure section 1218. Section 3769 protects the employee: no employer may use an assignment order as grounds for refusing to hire a person or for discharging or taking disciplinary action against an employee, and an employer who violates the section may be assessed a civil penalty of a maximum of five hundred dollars. Section 3771 adds an information channel: on request of the local child support agency the employer must provide, within 30 days, the absent parent's social security number and home address, whether the parent has a health insurance policy and if so the policy names and numbers and the persons covered, and whether the policy covers dependent children who do not live in the parent's home; subdivision (e) then requires the employer to notify the agency of any subsequent lapse in coverage, with the date coverage ended, the reason, and the expected resumption date if the lapse is temporary.

expectedJSON.body: Section 3773 creates a parallel track that applies only to Title IV-D cases in which support enforcement services are being provided by the local child support agency under Family Code section 17400. In those cases, after the court has ordered a parent to provide health insurance coverage, the local child support agency serves on the employer a national medical support notice in lieu of the health insurance coverage assignment order, and that notice may be combined with the order/notice to withhold income for child support authorized by Family Code section 5246. The notice has the same force and effect as a health insurance coverage assignment order, and the obligor has the same right to move to quash or terminate it as Article 2 gives for an assignment order. Section 3760(d) identifies where the notice comes from: it is the notice required by 42 U.S.C. section 666(a)(19) with respect to an order made under section 3773. That federal subsection requires state procedures under which all child support orders enforced under Part D include a provision for medical support for the child to be provided by either or both parents, enforced where appropriate through the National Medical Support Notice, and under which, where the obligated parent's employer is known to the State agency, the State agency uses the Notice to transfer notice of the health care coverage provision to the employer and the employer must transfer the Notice to the appropriate plan within 20 business days of its date. The Employee Retirement Income Security Act supplies the effect on the plan: under 29 U.S.C. section 1169(a)(5)(C), where the plan administrator of a group health plan maintained by or contributed to by the employer of a noncustodial parent receives an appropriately completed National Medical Support Notice that meets the requirements of paragraphs (3) and (4) of that subsection, the Notice is deemed to be a qualified medical child support order, and the administrator has 40 business days after the date of the Notice to act on it.

expectedJSON.gap: Family Code sections 3773 and 3760 were fetched from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and law.onecle.com, independent publishers that agree word for word; section 3773 and section 3760 were both last amended by Statutes 2000, chapter 119, before onecle's snapshot. The two federal sections were fetched from two genuinely independent publishers: the Office of the Law Revision Counsel's United States Code at uscode.house.gov and the Legal Information Institute at law.cornell.edu. Their texts agree in substance, and every quotation below was confirmed to be a verbatim substring of both after whitespace collapsing. They do not agree character for character in rendering, and that is disclosed rather than smoothed: the Law Revision Counsel prints a hyphen where the Legal Information Institute prints an em dash, and the Legal Information Institute's hyperlinking inserts spaces that the Law Revision Counsel does not have, so that 29 U.S.C. section 1169(a)(5)(A)(i) reads "the plan' s procedures" on the Legal Information Institute page and "the plan's procedures" at uscode.house.gov, and 42 U.S.C. section 666(a)(19)(B) reads "child support order )" on the former and "child support order)" on the latter. The quotations chosen here avoid every such point; no quotation spans a dash or a bracketed cross-reference. The National Medical Support Notice itself, the federal form bearing OMB control number 0970-0222 that form FL-478 names, was not fetched for this sheet and is not quoted. Section 3773(b) permits the notice to be combined with the order/notice to withhold income authorized by Family Code section 5246, a section that was not fetched and is named only as section 3773 names it. Section 3773(d) gives the obligor "the same right to move to quash or terminate" but does not state from what date the 15-day period in section 3765(b) runs when the instrument served is a national medical support notice rather than an assignment order delivered under section 3764(b); no authority resolving that was located. A CourtListener opinion search for the exact phrase "national medical support notice" returned a count of two, and neither result is a California decision or is quoted here: Franklin Electric Co. v. Lutheran Hospital of Indiana, Indiana Court of Appeals, decided March 31, 2010, and State v. Burke, Court of Appeals of North Carolina, decided August 7, 2007. Neither opinion was fetched, and out-of-state intermediate appellate authority is in any event not quoted in this sheet.
